study_identification.title: Mapping the Heterogeneous Phenotype of Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder Using Normative Models

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate the degree to which case-control analyses disguise interindividual differences in brain structure among patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and to map the brain alterations linked to these disorders at the level of individual patients.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT12; SPM-12; VBM-SPM12; 8mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing; FreeSurfer v5.3 (for supplementary analyses); 10mm FWHM surface-based smoothing

quality_checking_detail.reason: The study employed the 'weighted overall image quality' metric provided by the CAT12 toolbox. All participants scored < 2.8 on this metric (lower scores denote higher quality), with 99.1% of scans rated as 'good' and 0.9% as 'satisfactory'. The quality metric is sensitive to head motion and other image quality factors.
quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: Regarding image quality, we carefully checked the quality of all MRI scans included in our model using the 'weighted overall image quality' metric provided by the CAT12 toolbox. Whilst this does not assess the effect of head motion directly, it provides a reasonable estimate of overall image quality which is influenced by head motion. On this metric, all participants included in our cohort scored < 2.8, where lower scores denote higher image quality. On the rating scale provided by the authors of this tool (see www.neuro.uni-jena.de/cat/index.html#QA), this corresponds to a rating of 'good' for 99.1% of our scans and a small number (0.9%) as 'satisfactory'.
quality_checking_detail.location: Supplementary material, eMethods section on Potential confounding variables

site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The study was conducted at a single site (1.5 Tesla Siemens MAGNETOM Sonata scanner) with all participants recruited from the Oslo area, Norway. Therefore, site effect handling was not applicable.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: Structural scans were obtained on a 1.5 Tesla Siemens MAGNETOM Sonata scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) using a standard head coil. Patients were recruited from inpatient and outpatient clinics in the Oslo area of Norway. Healthy individuals from the same catchment area were drawn from the national population registry.
site_effect_handling_detail.location: Main text Methods section and Supplementary material eMethods section on MRI acquisition

response_variable.answer: Gray matter volume; White matter volume; Cortical thickness (supplementary); Pial area (supplementary)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and Sex modeled as fixed effects in GPR

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addressed image quality as a potential nuisance variable by using CAT12's weighted image quality metric and testing associations with deviations. They found a moderate positive correlation between extreme negative deviations in gray matter and lower image quality, but showed that diagnostic effects remained virtually the same with or without correction for image quality (β = 0.203 without correction vs β = 0.196 with correction). However, the authors acknowledge that their measure is relatively crude. The study also examined medication and substance abuse as potential confounds, but did not systematically model site effects (as it was a single-site study), heteroscedasticity, or other nuisance structure components comprehensively in the normative model itself.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Regarding image quality, the only significant association we detected was a moderate positive correlation with the percentage of extreme negative deviations in gray matter with overall image quality (i.e. more substantial negative deviations were associated with lower image quality). The image quality metric is quite general and is sensitive to many factors (e.g. head motion or pathology). Indeed, patients often move more in the scanner than controls. To better understand the nature of this variation, we performed two additional regression analyses to test if the explained variance between image quality measures and the reported diagnostic effect on the percentage of extreme negative deviations was shared. We could show that these effects are not shared, as the effect without correction for image quality measures of the diagnosis (β = 0.203; p < 0.001) was virtually the same as with correction (β = 0.196; p < 0.001). This gives us confidence that this has no significant impact on the main conclusions of this manuscript.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Supplementary material eResults section on Potential confounding variables

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validated the normative model using 10-fold cross-validation within the healthy control sample. This is a same-domain, non-independent validation approach where the training data is split and each fold is used for validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: To avoid overfitting in the normative models, it is crucial to estimate performance out of sample. Therefore, we estimated the normative range for this model in healthy individuals under 10-fold cross-validation, then applied the model trained on all data to patients.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text Methods section on Normative Modeling

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not use an independent hold-out dataset of healthy controls from the same domain for validation. All healthy controls from the TOP study were used in the 10-fold cross-validation procedure, with no separate independent validation cohort mentioned.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: All participants were recruited as part of the Thematically Organized Psychosis study from October 27, 2004, to October 17, 2012. We estimated the normative range for this model in healthy individuals under 10-fold cross-validation, then applied the model trained on all data to patients.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model on an external dataset from a different domain (different scanner, site, or cohort). All analyses were conducted on the single TOP study cohort.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: All participants were recruited as part of the Thematically Organized Psychosis study from October 27, 2004, to October 17, 2012. Data were reanalyzed in 2017 and 2018.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text Methods section on Participants

diseases_studied.answer: Schizophrenia (SCZ); Schizophrenia spectrum disorders (including Schizoaffective disorder and Schizophreniform disorder); Bipolar Disorder (BD)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (|z| > 2.6, P < .005 for extreme deviations); Percentage of extreme positive and extreme negative deviating voxels relative to total intracerebral voxels; FDR correction (supplementary analysis)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Chi-square tests comparing percentage of extreme deviations across diagnostic groups (corrected for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni-Holm method); Linear regressions testing associations between percentage of extremely deviating voxels and age, disease duration, and cognitive performance (verbal learning and memory, processing speed, working memory, executive functioning); Bonferroni-Holm correction for n=12 regressions within each disorder and modality; PALM (Permutation Analysis of Linear Models) for group-level deviation maps using t-tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement and modality correction
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: At the individual level, deviations from the normative model were frequent in both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder but highly heterogeneous, with overlap of more than 2% among patients observed in only a few loci, suggesting that the idea of the average patient is a noninformative construct in psychiatry.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: At the group level, patients with schizophrenia had significantly reduced gray matter in frontal regions, cerebellum, and temporal cortex, with mean deviations also more negative than in patients with bipolar disorder, primarily in frontal brain regions. In patients with bipolar disorder, mean deviations were primarily present in cerebellar regions. However, at the individual level, deviations were highly heterogeneous. In gray matter, patients with schizophrenia had 0.9% of voxels with extreme negative deviations compared to 0.23% in healthy controls (P < .001, Wald χ² = 219.67) and 0.24% in bipolar disorder patients (P < .001). For white matter, patients with schizophrenia had 0.62% extreme negative deviations compared to 0.25% in controls (P < .001) and 0.41% in bipolar patients (P = .001). Spatial overlap analysis revealed that only a few brain loci had extreme deviations in more than 2% of patients with the same disorder. Individual extreme deviations were linked to cognitive performance (particularly processing speed and executive functioning in bipolar disorder: β = -0.232, P = 0.001 for both after correction) and disorder duration (positive white matter deviations associated with disease duration in schizophrenia: β = 0.233, P = 0.003, corrected P = 0.036), but not to age. Supplementary analyses using FreeSurfer-derived cortical thickness and pial area measures produced nearly identical results, showing that extreme deviations were principally attributable to cortical thinning.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The study does not permit strong inferences about the degree to which certain confounding variables may have influenced findings. While no evidence of confounding effects of medication was found, minor associations between overall image quality and substance abuse with negative deviations in gray matter for schizophrenia were observed. However, the measures used to assess these effects are crude, and the study design does not permit inferences about the direction of causality (e.g., patients with greater severity may move more in the scanner and be more prone to drug abuse). The study was conducted at a single site, which limits generalizability. The normative model was not validated on external independent datasets from different domains.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study employed both fixed threshold (|z| > 2.6) and FDR correction approaches for individual deviation maps, with results remaining consistent across methods. The authors emphasize that their findings suggest that biological stratification of mental disorders, if useful, is likely to involve smaller strata than previously anticipated due to vast interindividual differences. They note that applying clustering algorithms to deviations from normative models to find subtypes would be best performed in larger samples and requires extensive validation. Importantly, they checked for potential confounding effects of scanner artifacts (head motion via image quality metrics), medication load (normalized total medication load), and substance abuse, finding that these did not substantially affect their main conclusions. The study also performed supplementary analyses using FreeSurfer-derived measures which corroborated the VBM findings.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a seminal paper in the field of normative modeling for psychiatry, demonstrating the limitations of traditional case-control designs in capturing individual-level heterogeneity. The study used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) as the primary processing framework rather than FreeSurfer to treat subcortical, cerebellar, and cortical structures consistently, though FreeSurfer analyses were included in supplementary materials. All cognitive measures had missing values imputed by the mean (imputation rates: 6.2-6.6%). The study included detailed characterization of medication use across groups (e.g., 79.1% of schizophrenia patients on antipsychotics vs 38.9% of bipolar patients; 18.4% of bipolar patients on lithium vs 1.2% of schizophrenia patients). Two T1-weighted scans were acquired for each participant and averaged after rigid registration to improve signal-to-noise ratio. The weighted overall image quality metric from CAT12 was used for quality control, with all participants scoring < 2.8 (lower is better). The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical Research Ethics and the Norwegian Data Inspectorate. Participants with schizophrenia spectrum disorders included 163 with pure schizophrenia, 33 with schizoaffective disorder, and 22 with schizophreniform disorder. Diagnosis was established using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I Disorders (SCID). The normative model was characterized by global gray matter decrease from 20 to 70 years of age, particularly in frontal and cerebellar regions, while white matter showed both decreases and increases across the adult lifetime.
